claim: The spinal cord is composed of distinct cell populations, mainly neurons and glial cells.
source: The spinal cord is composed of distinct cell populations, mainly neurons and glial cells (Abraira et al., 2017; Peirs and Seal, 2016; Todd, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Abraira et al., 2017; Peirs and Seal, 2016; Todd, 2017).

claim: The heterogeneity among the various neuronal clusters contributes to the differences in sensory perception, transduction, and processing, as well as the modulation of motor behaviors.
source: The heterogeneity among the various neuronal clusters contributes to the differences in sensory perception, transduction, and processing, as well as the modulation of motor behaviors (Abraira et al., 2017; Bourane et al., 2015; Floriddia et al., 2020; Hayashi et al., 2018; Mishra and Hoon, 2013; Todd, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Abraira et al., 2017; Bourane et al., 2015; Floriddia et al., 2020; Hayashi et al., 2018; Mishra and Hoon, 2013; Todd, 2010).

claim: Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing has provided an unbiased comprehensive strategy to explore gene expression at high resolution and classify cellular clusters in an objective manner.
source: Recently, single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has provided an unbiased comprehensive strategy to explore gene expression at high resolution and classify cellular clusters in an objective manner (Aldinger et al., 2021; Li et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Aldinger et al., 2021; Li et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2021).

claim: Single-nucleus analysis has several advantages, such as easy performance in whole tissue and avoidance of experimental artifacts in intact cells that are induced during the tissue dissociation process.
source: In particular, single-nucleus analysis has several advantages, such as easy performance in whole tissue and avoidance of experimental artifacts in intact cells that are induced during the tissue dissociation process (Grindberg et al., 2013; Habib et al., 2017; Lake et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Grindberg et al., 2013; Habib et al., 2017; Lake et al., 2016).

claim: Rosenberg et al. identified 30 neuronal types in the developing spinal cord of mice using split pool ligation-based transcriptome single-nucleus sequencing (SPLiT-seq).
source: Using split pool ligation-based transcriptome single-nucleus sequencing (SPLiT-seq), Rosenberg et al. identified 30 neuronal types in the developing spinal cord of mice (Rosenberg et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Rosenberg et al., 2018).

claim: Delile et al. performed high-throughput single-cell RNA-seq and revealed the spatial and temporal dynamics of gene expression in the cervical and thoracic spinal cords of developing mice.
source: Delile et al. performed high-throughput single-cell RNA-seq and revealed the spatial and temporal dynamics of gene expression in the cervical and thoracic spinal cords of developing mice (Delile et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Delile et al., 2019).

claim: Häring et al. identified 15 excitatory and 15 inhibitory subtypes of sensory neurons in the spinal dorsal horn of mice using single-cell RNA-seq.
source: Using single-cell RNA-seq, Häring et al. identified 15 excitatory and 15 inhibitory subtypes of sensory neurons in the spinal dorsal horn of mice (Häring et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Häring et al., 2018).

claim: Sathyamurthy et al. used massively parallel single-nucleus RNA-seq and identified 43 neuronal populations in the lumbar spinal cord of adult mice.
source: Sathyamurthy et al. used massively parallel single-nucleus RNA-seq and identified 43 neuronal populations in the lumbar spinal cord of adult mice (Sathyamurthy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Sathyamurthy et al., 2018).

claim: Russ et al. provided an integrated view of cell types in the mouse spinal cord and their spatial organization and gene expression signatures using single-cell RNA-seq.
source: Russ et al. provided an integrated view of cell types in the mouse spinal cord and their spatial organization and gene expression signatures using single-cell RNA-seq (Russ et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Russ et al., 2021).

claim: Recent studies have provided the single-cell transcriptomic profiles of the developing spinal cord in humans.
source: Recent studies have also provided the single-cell transcriptomic profiles of the developing spinal cord in humans (Andersen et al., 2023; Rayon et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Andersen et al., 2023; Rayon et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).

claim: Limited research has defined the heterogeneity among neurons and their spatial distribution in the adult human spinal cord at a single-cell resolution.
source: Although the molecular and cellular organization of the spinal cord neurons is relatively well understood in mice or developing humans, limited research has defined the heterogeneity among neurons and their spatial distribution in the adult human spinal cord at a single-cell resolution, which is important for understanding the molecular basis of spinal cord diseases and physiology because multiple findings from animal experiments cannot be directly replicated in humans (Kushnarev et al., 2020; Yekkirala et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kushnarev et al., 2020; Yekkirala et al., 2017).

claim: Multiple findings from animal experiments cannot be directly replicated in humans.
source: Although the molecular and cellular organization of the spinal cord neurons is relatively well understood in mice or developing humans, limited research has defined the heterogeneity among neurons and their spatial distribution in the adult human spinal cord at a single-cell resolution, which is important for understanding the molecular basis of spinal cord diseases and physiology because multiple findings from animal experiments cannot be directly replicated in humans (Kushnarev et al., 2020; Yekkirala et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kushnarev et al., 2020; Yekkirala et al., 2017).

claim: This study classified human spinal cord neurons into 21 subtypes with distinct transcriptional patterns, molecular markers, and functional annotations.
source: As a result, we classified human spinal cord neurons into 21 subtypes with distinct transcriptional patterns, molecular markers, and functional annotations.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including single-nucleus RNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics results.

claim: The overall molecular and cellular organization of the human spinal cord are similar to those reported in mice, although some degree of heterogeneity among transcriptional patterns exists.
source: The resulting atlas demonstrates that the overall molecular and cellular organization of the human spinal cord are similar to those reported in mice, although some degree of heterogeneity among transcriptional patterns exists.
evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis between human and mouse data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Several genes showed sex differences in motor neurons.
source: In addition, we determined that several genes showed sex differences in motor neurons.
evidence: Supported by the sex difference analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: A publicly available website (https://zhangdhscu.shinyapps.io/spinal/) was set up based on the sequencing data.
source: More importantly, we set up a publicly available website (https://zhangdhscu.shinyapps.io/spinal/) based on our sequencing data, which will be convenient to search genes of interest.
evidence: Supported by the statement in the manuscript about the creation of the website.

claim: Using the 10x Genomics Visium Spatial Gene Expression platform, spatial transcriptomes were generated for spinal cells of lumbar enlargements from six adult human donors (three males and three females, 47–59 years old).
source: Using the 10x Genomics Visium Spatial Gene Expression platform, we generated spatial transcriptomes for spinal cells of lumbar enlargements from six adult human donors (three males and three females, 47–59 years old) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by the experimental methods described and Figure 1A showing the workflow.

claim: 17 cellular types were initially identified from the spatial transcriptomics data.
source: From these spots, we initially identified 17 cellular types (Figure 1B) with distinct distribution characteristics in the spinal slices (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by the experimental data and Figure 1B showing the UMAP plot of 17 cell types.

claim: The 17 cell types were classified into five major clusters: neurons, Schwann cells, a mixed population of neurons and astrocytes, a mixed population of meningeal and vascular cells, and a mixed population of glial cells (oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocyte precursor cells).
source: Based on the representative marker genes (Figure 1D and E), these 17 cell types were classified into five major clusters, including neurons, Schwann cells, a mixed population of neurons and astrocytes, a mixed population of meningeal and vascular cells, and a mixed population of glial cells (oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocyte precursor cells) (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by the experimental data and Figures 1D, 1E, 1F, and 1G showing marker gene expression and cell type classification.

claim: A large portion of neurons were not well separated from their surrounding astrocytes due to the lower resolution of the spatial transcriptomic approach.
source: Because of the lower resolution of the spatial transcriptomic approach than that of single-cell or single-nucleus transcriptomes, a large portion of neurons were not well separated from their surrounding astrocytes.
evidence: Supported by the technical limitations of the spatial transcriptomics method described in the manuscript.

claim: Each individual donor contributed spots to each cluster in the spatial transcriptomics data.
source: We verified that each individual donor contributed spots to each cluster (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by the verification described and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single-nucleus RNA-seq was performed on 64,021 nuclei from the lumbar enlargements of the spinal cord from nine adult humans (six males and three females, 35–59 years old).
source: To obtain single-cell resolution, we further performed single-nucleus RNA-seq on 64,021 nuclei from the lumbar enlargements of the spinal cord from nine adult humans (six males and three females, 35–59 years old), including the same six donors used in spatial transcriptomics (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by the experimental methods described and Figure 2A showing the workflow.

claim: Eight major cell types were identified from the single-nucleus RNA-seq data: oligodendrocytes (58.8% of total nuclei), microglia (13.1% of total nuclei), neurons (11.9% of total nuclei), astrocytes (5.2% of total nuclei), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (4.6% of total nuclei), vascular cells (3% of total nuclei), meningeal cells (2.1% of total nuclei), and Schwann cells (1.2% of total nuclei).
source: As a result, eight major cell types (Figure 2B) were identified with distinct molecular markers (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B): oligodendrocytes (58.8% of total nuclei), microglia (13.1% of total nuclei), neurons (11.9% of total nuclei), astrocytes (5.2% of total nuclei), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (4.6% of total nuclei), vascular cells (3% of total nuclei), meningeal cells (2.1% of total nuclei), and Schwann cells (1.2% of total nuclei).
evidence: Supported by the experimental data and Figures 2B, 2C, 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Each individual donor contributed cells to each cluster and no individual donor was responsible for any specific cluster in the single-nucleus RNA-seq data.
source: We verified that each individual donor contributed cells to each cluster and that no individual donor was responsible for any specific cluster (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by the verification described and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: On average, 5245 genes were detected in a single spinal cord neuron, and 2241 genes were detected in a single non-neuron cell.
source: The number of genes detected per nucleus varied among the major cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D). On average, 5245 genes were detected in a single spinal cord neuron, and 2241 genes were detected in a single non-neuron cell.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Neurons mainly existed in gray matter, while oligodendrocytes and microglia were mainly present in white matter.
source: The results showed that neurons mainly existed in gray matter, while oligodendrocytes and microglia were mainly present in white matter (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by the spatial mapping data and Figure 2E showing the spatial distribution.

claim: Astrocytes were widely present in the spinal cord but were more highly expressed in the white matter than in the gray matter.
source: Astrocytes were widely present in the spinal cord but were more highly expressed in the white matter than in the gray matter (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by the spatial mapping data and Figure 2E showing the spatial distribution.

claim: The spatial distribution of neurons, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and astrocytes was validated using immunofluorescence staining.
source: These findings were validated using IF staining (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by the immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: 7641 neuronal nuclei were reclassified into 21 subclusters based on their transcriptional characteristics.
source: To identify and characterize various neuronal subtypes within the spinal cord, 7641 neuronal nuclei were reclassified into 21 subclusters (Figure 3A) based on their transcriptional characteristics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by the experimental data and Figure 3A showing the UMAP plot of 21 neuronal clusters.

claim: According to the neurotransmitter status, 11 subclusters (54.4%) were defined as excitatory neuronal sets (glutamatergic, with markers of SLC17A6), 8 subclusters (34.5%) were inhibitory neurons (GABAergic/glycinergic, with markers of GAD1, GAD2, and SLC6A5), 1 subcluster (9.6%) expressed both excitatory and inhibitory markers, and 1 subcluster (1.5%) was motor neurons (cholinergic, with markers of CHAT and SLC5A7).
source: According to the neurotransmitter status, 11 subclusters (54.4%) were defined as excitatory neuronal sets (glutamatergic, with markers of SLC17A6), 8 subclusters (34.5%) were inhibitory neurons (GABAergic/glycinergic, with markers of GAD1, GAD2, and SLC6A5), 1 subcluster (9.6%) expressed both excitatory and inhibitory markers, and 1 subcluster (1.5%) was motor neurons (cholinergic, with markers of CHAT and SLC5A7) (Figure 3B and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by the experimental data and Figures 3B, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Gene Ontology term analysis showed that the overall functional assignments for excitatory, inhibitory, and motor clusters were similar in the adult human spinal cord.
source: We found that the overall functional assignments for excitatory, inhibitory, and motor clusters were similar in the adult human spinal cord (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), such as chemical or glutamatergic synaptic transmission, axon guidance, neuron projection development, glutamate receptor signaling pathway, regulation of NMDA receptor activity, and ion transmembrane transport, suggesting that these neuronal subpopulations cooperated in the regulation of spinal functions.
evidence: Supported by the Gene Ontology analysis and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory neurons were predominantly mapped to the dorsal horn.
source: Excitatory (Figure 3F) and inhibitory (Figure 3G) neurons were predominantly mapped to the dorsal horn, which was confirmed by IF staining of their markers.
evidence: Supported by the spatial mapping data and immunofluorescence staining shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: Motor neurons (CHAT positive) were predominantly located in the ventral horn, with scattered expression in the dorsal horn.
source: Motor neurons (CHAT positive) were predominantly located in the ventral horn, with scattered expression in the dorsal horn (Figure 3H), which is consistent with the recent published study (Yadav et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by the spatial mapping data shown in Figure 3H and citation to published literature (Yadav et al., 2023).

claim: Gene set variation analysis indicated that C3, C4, C6, C7, C8, C10, and C13–19 clusters were predominantly present in the superficial dorsal horn; C1, C2, and C12 clusters were in the deep dorsal horn, C5, C9, and C11 clusters were present across the superficial and deep dorsal horn, while C0 and C20 clusters were mainly located in the ventral horn.
source: For specific clusters, gene set variation analysis (GSVA) indicated that C3, C4, C6, C7, C8, C10, and C13–19 clusters were predominantly present in the SD; C1, C2, and C12 clusters were in the DD, C5, C9, and C11 clusters were present across the SD and the DD, while C0 and C20 clusters were mainly located in the ventral horn (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by the gene set variation analysis and Figures 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: C8 was mapped to the superficial dorsal horn, and its representative marker, PDYN (prodynorphin), was distributed primarily in laminae I–II.
source: For example, C8 was mapped to the superficial dorsal horn, and its representative marker, PDYN (prodynorphin, ligands for the kappa-type of opioid receptor), was distributed primarily in laminae I–II (Figure 3J), consistent with the previously reported location of PDYN-expressing neurons in the rodent spinal cord (Duan et al., 2014; Sapio et al., 2020; Serafin et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by the spatial mapping data and immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 3J, and citations to published literature (Duan et al., 2014; Sapio et al., 2020; Serafin et al., 2019).

claim: CCK (cholecystokinin) was widely present in human dorsal glutamatergic neurons, consistent with the findings in mice.
source: For instance, CCK (cholecystokinin, involved in sensory processing under physiological and pain conditions) (Liu et al., 2018; Peirs et al., 2021; Figure 3—figure supplement 6A–D) and SST (somatostatin, involved in transmitting itch and pain sensation) (Fatima et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Figure 3—figure supplement 6E–H) were widely present in human dorsal glutamatergic neurons, consistent with the findings in mice (Todd, 2017).
evidence: Supported by the immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6A–D and citations to published literature (Liu et al., 2018; Peirs et al., 2021; Todd, 2017).

claim: SST (somatostatin) was widely present in human dorsal glutamatergic neurons, consistent with the findings in mice.
source: For instance, CCK (cholecystokinin, involved in sensory processing under physiological and pain conditions) (Liu et al., 2018; Peirs et al., 2021; Figure 3—figure supplement 6A–D) and SST (somatostatin, involved in transmitting itch and pain sensation) (Fatima et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Figure 3—figure supplement 6E–H) were widely present in human dorsal glutamatergic neurons, consistent with the findings in mice (Todd, 2017).
evidence: Supported by the immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6E–H and citations to published literature (Fatima et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Todd, 2017).

claim: FOXP2 (Forkhead box P2) was presented in both human glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons.
source: FOXP2 (Forkhead box P2, involved neuronal differentiation and movement disorders) (Rousso et al., 2012) was presented in both human glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 6I–L).
evidence: Supported by the immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6I–L and citation to published literature (Rousso et al., 2012).

claim: The neuronal data of the human spinal cord overlapped well with those from the mouse in the uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP).
source: Overall, the neuronal data of the human spinal cord overlapped well with those from the mouse in the uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis and Figure 4A showing the coclustering of mouse and human neurons.

claim: Homologous clusters between humans and mice showed a highly similar transcriptional profile.
source: To more directly compare the single-nucleus RNA-seq data from human and mouse spinal cord, homologous clusters between humans and mice were identified (Figure 4B) using the methods as previously described (Nguyen et al., 2021), which showed a highly similar transcriptional profile between species (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis and Figures 4B and 4C, and citation to published literature (Nguyen et al., 2021).

claim: Shared representative genes for several homologous neuronal clusters in humans and mice include ZFHX3 or Zfhx3 for C2, SOX5 or Sox5 for C4, and GRM3 or Grm3 for C9.
source: We found shared representative genes for several homologous neuronal clusters in humans and mice, such as ZFHX3 or Zfhx3 (zinc finger homeobox 3) for C2, SOX5 or Sox5 (SRY-box transcription factor 5) for C4, and GRM3 or Grm3 (glutamate receptor, metabotropic 3) for C9.
evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis of gene expression between human and mouse data.

claim: The transcriptional patterns were similar between human and mouse spinal cords for several genes, including CHRM3 or Chrm3, NRXN3 or Nrxn3, NXPH1 or Nhpx1, DSCAML1 or Dscaml1, CACNA2D3 or Cacna2d3, and GRIK1 or Grik1 predominantly expressed in inhibitory clusters.
source: The transcriptional patterns were similar between human and mouse spinal cords, such as CHRM3 or Chrm3 (cholinergic receptor muscarinic 3), NRXN3 or Nrxn3 (neurexin 3), NXPH1 or Nhpx1 (neurexophilin 1), DSCAML1 or Dscaml1 (DS cell adhesion molecule like 1), CACNA2D3 or Cacna2d3 (calcium voltage-gated channel auxiliary subunit alpha 2 delta 3), and GRIK1 or Grik1 (glutamate ionotropic receptor kainate type subunit 1) were predominantly expressed in inhibitory clusters, and CACNA2D1 or Cacna2d1 (calcium voltage-gated channel auxiliary subunit alpha 2 delta 1), EBF1 or Ebf1 (EBF transcription factor 1), EBF2 or Ebf2 (EBF transcription factor 2), CPNE4 or Cpne4 (copine 4), CPNE8 or Cpne8 (copine 8), MAML3 or Maml3 (mastermind like transcriptional coactivator 3), PDE11A or Pde11a (phosphodiesterase 11A), SOX5 or Sox5 (SRY-box transcription factor 5), and ERBB4 or Erbb4 (erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4) were predominantly expressed in excitatory clusters.
evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis of gene expression between human and mouse data.

claim: CACNA2D1 or Cacna2d1, EBF1 or Ebf1, EBF2 or Ebf2, CPNE4 or Cpne4, CPNE8 or Cpne8, MAML3 or Maml3, PDE11A or Pde11a, SOX5 or Sox5, and ERBB4 or Erbb4 were predominantly expressed in excitatory clusters in both human and mouse spinal cords.
source: The transcriptional patterns were similar between human and mouse spinal cords, such as CHRM3 or Chrm3 (cholinergic receptor muscarinic 3), NRXN3 or Nrxn3 (neurexin 3), NXPH1 or Nhpx1 (neurexophilin 1), DSCAML1 or Dscaml1 (DS cell adhesion molecule like 1), CACNA2D3 or Cacna2d3 (calcium voltage-gated channel auxiliary subunit alpha 2 delta 3), and GRIK1 or Grik1 (glutamate ionotropic receptor kainate type subunit 1) were predominantly expressed in inhibitory clusters, and CACNA2D1 or Cacna2d1 (calcium voltage-gated channel auxiliary subunit alpha 2 delta 1), EBF1 or Ebf1 (EBF transcription factor 1), EBF2 or Ebf2 (EBF transcription factor 2), CPNE4 or Cpne4 (copine 4), CPNE8 or Cpne8 (copine 8), MAML3 or Maml3 (mastermind like transcriptional coactivator 3), PDE11A or Pde11a (phosphodiesterase 11A), SOX5 or Sox5 (SRY-box transcription factor 5), and ERBB4 or Erbb4 (erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4) were predominantly expressed in excitatory clusters.
evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis of gene expression between human and mouse data.

claim: SLC5A7 or Slc5a7, SLIT3 or Slit3, CREB5 or Creb5, and PRUNE2 or Prune2 were predominantly expressed in motor neurons in both human and mouse spinal cords.
source: SLC5A7 or Slc5a7 (solute carrier family 5 member 7), SLIT3 or Slit3 (slit guidance ligand 3), CREB5 or Creb5 (cAMP responsive element binding protein 5), and PRUNE2 or Prune2 (prune homolog 2) were predominantly expressed in motor neurons.
evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis of gene expression between human and mouse data.

claim: Differential expression between excitatory and inhibitory neurons was observed for a pair of calcium channels (CACNA2D1 or Cacna2d1, and CACNA2D3 or Cacna2d3) in humans and mice.
source: As expected, genes associated with neurotransmitter status were identified (such as GAD1, Gad2, Slc6a1, Chat, SLC5A7, and Slc5a7), but we also observed differential expression between excitatory and inhibitory neurons for a pair of calcium channels (CACNA2D1 or Cacna2d1, and CACNA2D3 or Cacna2d3) in humans and mice.
evidence: Supported by the comparative analysis of gene expression between human and mouse data.

claim: The findings regarding differential expression of calcium channels were consistent with a previous study.
source: These findings were consistent with a previous study (Russ et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Russ et al., 2021).

claim: The expression of SST was significantly higher in C13 than in other clusters of humans.
source: For example, the expression of SST was significantly higher in C13 than in other clusters of humans (Figure 4D and F), and the expression of NPY (neuropeptide Y, which influences many physiological processes, such as cortical excitability and stress response) was higher in C11 than in other clusters of humans (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claim: The expression of NPY (neuropeptide Y) was higher in C11 than in other clusters of humans.
source: For example, the expression of SST was significantly higher in C13 than in other clusters of humans (Figure 4D and F), and the expression of NPY (neuropeptide Y, which influences many physiological processes, such as cortical excitability and stress response) was higher in C11 than in other clusters of humans (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claim: In the mouse spinal cord, Nts (neurotensin) showed selectively higher expression levels in C13.
source: In the mouse spinal cord, Nts (neurotensin that may function as a neurotransmitter or a neuromodulator) and Nos1 (nitric oxide synthase 1 that functions as a neurotransmitter) showed selectively higher expression levels in C13 and C8, respectively (Figure 4E and G).
evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4E and 4G.

claim: In the mouse spinal cord, Nos1 (nitric oxide synthase 1) showed selectively higher expression levels in C8.
source: In the mouse spinal cord, Nts (neurotensin that may function as a neurotransmitter or a neuromodulator) and Nos1 (nitric oxide synthase 1 that functions as a neurotransmitter) showed selectively higher expression levels in C13 and C8, respectively (Figure 4E and G).
evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4E and 4G.

claim: TAC1 (tachykinin precursor 1) and NPY were mainly present in the clusters of superficial dorsal neurons of both human and mouse spinal cord.
source: For example, TAC1 (tachykinin precursor 1, functions as a neurotransmitter) and NPY were mainly present in the clusters (e.g., C4 and C11, respectively) of superficial dorsal neurons of both human (Figure 4D and F) and mouse spinal cord (Figure 4E and G), which were confirmed by RNAscope ISH and/or IF staining (Figure 4H–K).
evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D, 4E, 4F, and 4G, and RNAscope ISH and IF staining shown in Figures 4H–K.

claim: Calca (calcitonin-related polypeptide alpha) was selectively expressed in C20 of mice.
source: For example, Calca (calcitonin-related polypeptide alpha, which is involved in migraine) was selectively expressed in C20 of mice (Figure 4E and G), but CALCA almost did not exist in human spinal neurons (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D, 4E, 4F, and 4G.

claim: CALCA almost did not exist in human spinal neurons.
source: For example, Calca (calcitonin-related polypeptide alpha, which is involved in migraine) was selectively expressed in C20 of mice (Figure 4E and G), but CALCA almost did not exist in human spinal neurons (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claim: GRP (gastrin releasing peptide) was predominantly present in C7 of humans.
source: GRP (gastrin releasing peptide) was predominantly present in C7 of humans (Figure 4D and F), but Grp showed little expression in all mouse spinal neuronal clusters (Figure 4E and G).
evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claim: Grp showed little expression in all mouse spinal neuronal clusters.
source: GRP (gastrin releasing peptide) was predominantly present in C7 of humans (Figure 4D and F), but Grp showed little expression in all mouse spinal neuronal clusters (Figure 4E and G).
evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4E and 4G.

claim: Several genes, such as PAM, OPRM1, EBF1, GABRG3, GRIK2, SCN1A, KCND2, and RORA, were highly and widely expressed in the spinal neurons of both humans and mice.
source: Of note, several genes, such as PAM (peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase), OPRM1 (opioid receptor mu 1), EBF1, GABRG3 (gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor subunit gamma3), GRIK2 (glutamate ionotropic receptor kainate type subunit 2), SCN1A (sodium voltage-gated channel alpha subunit 1), KCND2 (potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily D member 2), and RORA (RAR related orphan receptor A), were highly and widely expressed in the spinal neurons of both humans and mice (Figure 4D and G, Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3), which may provide some guidance for future studies that focus translational efforts on conserved molecular targets across species.
evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D, 4G, and Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Several genes, such as CALCA, GAL, and NPR1, showed little expression in the human spinal cord.
source: However, several genes, such as CALCA, GAL (galanin), and NPR1 (natriuretic peptide receptor 1), showed little expression in the human spinal cord (Figure 4D and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3J–L), which should be considered during clinical translation.
evidence: Supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4D, 4F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3J–L.

claim: Neuronal barcodes from both sexes were represented in all subclusters, suggesting that males and females have the same spinal neuronal subtypes.
source: Neuronal barcodes from both sexes were represented in all subclusters, suggesting that males and females have the same spinal neuronal subtypes (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by the sex difference analysis and Figure 5A showing barcodes from males and females in all clusters.

claim: The comparative results showed similar gene expression profiles between male and female spinal neuronal clusters, except for C20 (motor neurons).
source: The comparative results showed similar gene expression profiles between male and female spinal neuronal clusters (Figure 5B), except for C20 (motor neurons) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by the sex difference analysis and Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: C20 (motor neurons) had the highest number of differentially expressed genes between males and females.
source: C20 (motor neurons) had the highest number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (Figure 5C), suggesting potential molecular differences in mechanisms of motor function between men and women.
evidence: Supported by the sex difference analysis and Figure 5C.

claim: In C20 (motor neurons), males showed higher expression of genes that encode potassium channels and lower expression of genes that encode sodium channels compared to females.
source: A main finding in C20 was the higher expression of genes that encode potassium channels, whereas a lower expression of genes that encode sodium channels was found in males compared to females (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by the sex difference analysis and Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: The finding of higher expression of genes encoding potassium channels and lower expression of genes encoding sodium channels in males compared to females in C20 was validated by immunofluorescence staining examining SCN10A expression in CHAT neurons from male and female donors.
source: This finding was validated in IF staining examining SCN10A (sodium voltage-gated channel alpha subunit 10) expression in CHAT neurons from male and female donors (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by the immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: Other genes encoding proteins associated with pain sensation were differentially expressed in C20 between male and female donors, such as HCN1, FGF13, LRFN5, HTR2C, and KCNQ3.
